how-much-to-charge-for-wash-and-fold.htm.text:
← Wash and fold price per pound calculator

How much should I charge for wash and fold?

Every quick answer to this is a range — a dollar to two-fifty a pound, more in cities. The range is not wrong, and it will not tell you whether your own minimum charge covers what a small order really costs, which is where most of the money is actually lost.

Open the free wash and fold calculator

What one order actually costs

A 22 lb order run on 0.9 labour minutes per pound, an $18.88 loaded wage, two 20 lb washers, one 30 lb dryer, two delivery stops, and a $2,400 monthly overhead spread across 6,000 lb comes to $31.79 — $1.445 a pound:

Cost componentPer orderPer pound
Labour$9.06$0.412
Machine cycles (2 wash, 1 dry)$3.80$0.173
Supplies$1.32$0.060
Pickup and delivery (2 stops)$8.81$0.401
Overhead share$8.80$0.400
Total cost$31.79$1.445
Charged at $1.75/lb$38.50$1.750
Profit (17.4% margin)$6.71$0.305

17.4% is above break-even and short of a healthy target. Hitting a 35% margin on these same costs needs $2.22 a pound instead of $1.75 — a 47 cent increase, not the couple of dimes it might feel like it should take.

Why your minimum charge might still lose money

Now price a 10 lb order at the same $1.75 a pound. The list price is $17.50, so a $20 minimum charge kicks in and looks generous. It is not checked against the actual cost of that order, which is where the trap is:

Line22 lb order10 lb order
Washer/dryer loads2 wash, 1 dry1 wash, 1 dry
Labour$9.06$5.66
Machine cycles$3.80$2.45
Supplies$1.32$0.60
Pickup and delivery (2 stops either way)$8.81$8.81
Overhead share$8.80$4.00
Total cost$31.79$21.52
Revenue at $1.75/lb, $20 minimum$38.50$20.00
Profit / (loss)$6.71($1.52)

The $20 minimum still loses $1.52 on this order. Intake, tagging, staging and checkout take nearly the same minutes on a 10 lb order as a 22 lb one, a pickup and a drop-off are two stops either way, and a half-full washer costs the same as a full one. A minimum charge only protects an order if it is set above what that order actually costs to process — here, $21.52, not $20. Round numbers picked by feel are the most common way a minimum ends up below cost.

What delivery adds to the price

Strip the two delivery stops out of the same 22 lb order and the cost drops from $31.79 to $22.98 — $1.045 a pound instead of $1.445. Delivery is adding about 40 cents a pound, roughly 28% of the total:

ServiceOrder costCost per pound
Counter service (0 stops)$22.98$1.045
Pickup and delivery (2 stops)$31.79$1.445
Difference$8.81$0.400

Because delivery cost is per stop, it falls per pound as an order gets bigger and rises per pound as it shrinks. A single per-pound rate across both counter and delivery customers means the delivery route is either underpriced or the counter is overpriced — a separate delivery fee or a route-specific rate is what usually fixes it.

How many more orders a profit goal actually needs

At 6,000 lb a month of 22 lb orders — about 273 orders — and $0.305 profit per pound, the numbers above net $1,830 a month. Reaching a $3,000 target is a volume question, not a pricing one, once the per-pound margin is already healthy:

FigureValue
Current monthly volume6,000 lb (~273 orders)
Current monthly profit$1,830
Target monthly profit$3,000
Volume needed for target9,837 lb (448 orders)
Additional orders needed175 a month (~40/week)

Forty more orders a week is a concrete thing to go find — another delivery day, a second driver, or a push on repeat customers — in a way "$1,170 more a month" is not. Seeing the order count is what turns a revenue gap into a plan.

Common questions

How much should I charge for wash and fold?

There is no single number, because the cost side varies far more than the price side. On a typical 22 lb order — 0.9 labour minutes per pound, $16 an hour loaded to $18.88, two 20 lb washers, one 30 lb dryer, two delivery stops, and a $2,400 monthly overhead spread across 6,000 lb — the order costs $31.79 to process, which is $1.445 a pound. Charging $1.75 a pound brings in $38.50 and profits $6.71, a 17.4% margin. Hitting a 35% margin target on the same costs needs $2.22 a pound instead. Work out your own cost per pound first, then set the price above it by the margin you need.

Why does my $20 minimum charge still lose money on a small order?

Because a minimum charge only works if it is set above the true cost of the smallest order it covers, and $20 sounds generous without ever being checked against that cost. A 10 lb order at the same $1.75 a pound would list at $17.50, so the $20 minimum kicks in and looks like it is protecting the order. But that 10 lb order still costs $21.52 to process — one washer, one dryer, the same two delivery stops, and the same per-order intake and tagging time that a 22 lb order also carries in full. The $20 minimum covers $17.50 of list price with room to spare and still loses $1.52 against the real cost. The minimum charge that actually breaks even on this order is $21.52, not $20.

How much does pickup and delivery add to the price per pound?

On the 22 lb example, two delivery stops (a pickup and a drop-off) cost $8.81 of the $31.79 order total — about $0.40 a pound, or 28% of the cost. Strip the delivery stops out and the same order costs $22.98 to process, or $1.045 a pound, against $1.445 a pound with delivery. Delivery cost is per stop, so it falls per pound as the order gets bigger and rises per pound as it shrinks — which is why a delivery route needs either a higher per-pound rate than counter service, a delivery fee, or a route minimum to cover the same stops on a smaller order.

How many more wash and fold orders does a profit goal actually need?

Divide the gap between your current monthly profit and your target by your profit per pound, then convert pounds to orders using your average order weight. At 6,000 lb a month of 22 lb orders — about 273 orders — and $0.305 profit per pound, the shop nets $1,830 a month. Reaching a $3,000 target needs 9,837 lb, which is 448 orders of that size: 175 more orders a month than today, or about 40 more a week. Seeing the order count rather than the dollar gap is what makes a target concrete, because orders are what has to fit on the intake counter and in the delivery route.

Run it on your own numbers

The calculator does this arithmetic on your own labour, machine, supply, delivery and overhead rates — not the illustrative figures above — and reports your cost per pound, break-even price, margin at what you charge today, and the volume a profit goal needs. It runs entirely in your browser.

A pricing calculator for laundromats and laundry pickup-and-delivery operators. What this does and doesn't do

This is arithmetic on numbers you supply: it totals what one order costs you and compares that to what one order earns. It does not know your water, sewer, gas or electricity tariff, your local wage rules, your machines' actual consumption, or what customers in your town will pay — every one of those is an input you read off your own bills, payroll and equipment specifications. Treat the output as the cost floor underneath your own pricing decision, not a recommended price.

Common questions

How much should I charge per pound for wash and fold?

There is no single right number, because the cost side varies more than the price side: a shop paying $0.09 a gallon for water with 40 lb washers has a different floor than one paying $0.02 with 20 lb machines. Work out your own cost per pound first — labour minutes, wash and dry cycles, supplies, any delivery stops, and a share of overhead — then set the price above it by the margin you need. This calculator does that arithmetic on your own numbers; what your market will bear is a separate question it cannot answer.

Why does a small wash and fold order lose money at the same price per pound?

Because a lot of the cost is per order rather than per pound. Intake, tagging, staging, bagging and checkout take the same minutes on a 10 lb order as on a 30 lb one, a pickup and a delivery are two stops either way, and a half-full washer costs a full cycle. Spread over ten pounds instead of thirty, those fixed costs are three times as heavy per pound — which is what a minimum charge exists to cover.

What should the wash cost per load include?

Everything one cycle consumes: water at your metered rate, sewer if it is billed on water volume, the gas or electricity to heat that water, the electricity the machine draws, and a wear-and-replacement allowance for the machine itself. Read the rates off your own utility bills and your machine's rated water consumption per cycle rather than a published average, because tariffs and machine efficiency differ enormously between towns and between machines.

Should pickup and delivery be priced into the per-pound rate or charged separately?

Either works, and the calculator shows why the choice matters: delivery cost is per stop, so it falls per pound as orders get bigger. Folding it into the per-pound rate means large orders subsidise small ones; charging a delivery fee or setting a route minimum puts the cost where it is incurred. Enter your stops per order, drive minutes and vehicle cost per mile to see how big the effect is at your average order weight.

Does anything I type here get uploaded?

No. Every calculation runs in this browser, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere — there are no accounts, no cookies, and no analytics vendor. If you use the save button, your numbers are written to this browser's own local storage on this device only, and the forget button deletes them. The Copy shareable link button puts the same numbers in the page's own URL fragment instead of a server, which your browser never sends anywhere. Anonymous feature counts (estimate, example_loaded, inputs_saved, link_copied) are stored the same local way and can be switched off.

vs-doing-the-cost-math-yourself.html.text:
← Wash and Fold Price Per Pound Calculator

This calculator vs. doing the cost math yourself

Machine cost plus a bit for labor, divided by a typical order's weight, is the estimate most laundromat and pickup-and-delivery operators reach for when it is time to set or reprice a per-pound rate. It is not wrong on the order it was built around — it is wrong on every order that is not that size.

What each approach actually does

Doing the math yourself usually starts from one typical order: what does a wash and a dry cycle cost, roughly how many minutes of labor, add a bit for supplies, divide by the pounds. That is a fair estimate for an order close to that exact size. It breaks down at the edges: a small drop-off still runs a full wash and dry cycle even if the machine is half empty, so the cost per pound on that order is much higher than the average implies. Intake, tagging and checkout take roughly the same few minutes whether the order is 8 pounds or 30, so that fixed cost gets diluted correctly only on the order it was estimated from. A delivery stop's drive time and mileage do not show up in a per-pound guess at all. And overhead — rent, insurance, the base utility bill, the card processor — is easy to leave out of a mental number entirely.

This calculator costs machine cycles as whole steps, not a smooth rate, so a partial load costs what it actually costs. It keeps per-pound costs (labor minutes, supplies) and per-order costs (fixed intake minutes, delivery stops) separate, so a small order is priced on what it consumes rather than an average across every order size. And it turns a monthly overhead figure and monthly volume into a per-pound share automatically, which is the step a hand-built estimate most often skips.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is a rough $1.75-a-pound guess close for my typical order?Often yes — that is the order the guess was built around.
What does a 10 lb drop-off actually cost once it still runs a full wash and dry cycle?This calculator — stepwise machine cost, not a smoothed per-pound rate.
Does my minimum charge cover the smallest order I accept?This calculator's minimum-charge finding, which costs that order size specifically.
How much of my price per pound needs to be overhead, not just touch cost?This calculator, once monthly overhead and monthly volume are entered.
Why does a small order or a delivery stop feel like it barely breaks even?This calculator's own pricing guide.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't a rough price per pound close enough?

For an average-sized order with no delivery stop, a careful rough estimate can land close. What it tends to miss is everything that does not scale evenly with weight: a small order still runs a full wash and dry cycle even if the machine is half empty, intake and tagging cost the same whether the order is 8 pounds or 30, a delivery stop costs the same drive time and mileage either way, and overhead (rent, insurance, the base utility bill) has to be spread across pounds somehow. Each of those pulls the true cost per pound on a small order well above the average the rough guess used.

What does this calculator do that mental math can't?

It costs machine cycles as whole steps rather than a smooth per-pound rate, so a partially filled washer or dryer shows up as the full cycle it actually costs. It separates per-pound costs (labor minutes, supplies) from per-order costs (fixed intake minutes, delivery stops) so a small order is priced on what it actually consumes rather than an average across all order sizes. And it turns monthly overhead and monthly volume into a per-pound share automatically, rather than leaving that step out entirely, which is the most common gap in a hand-built estimate.

When is a rough estimate the better choice?

When every order runs close to the same size, uses close to a full machine load, and never involves a delivery stop, a rough per-pound number and this calculator will land close together — there is little for the per-order and stepwise-machine effects to bite on. The calculator earns its keep on the order that is not typical: a small drop-off that still eats a full cycle, or a delivery route stop whose drive time and mileage do not show up in a flat per-pound guess at all.
